en: Preface to the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, composed by Xu Wa, Court Counselor and Acting County Registrar of Gaocheng County in Henan Prefecture during the Tang Dynasty.
Now, when the sun and moon rise, their brilliance illuminates the ten directions; when the seasonal rains descend, they cleanse and refresh all things. How much more so...
My body is eternally blissful, its appearance as profound and empty as space. Wondrous awakening is perfectly luminous, the essence that fuses the mind and its activities.

It is neither clamor nor obscurity; it is that which neither arises nor ceases. Therefore, the ground of no-more-learning was opened to cultivate the Kalandaka grove, and the ford where words cease was initiated to truly establish the city of Vārāṇasī.
Through the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya, the conditions of skillful means arose, and the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven...
A person who has developed the power of accomplishment—how could they be described by conventional names? Is this not the primary truth (*paramārtha*)?
Since the constellations were eclipsed by night and the immortal rainbow blazed by day, the blue bowl transmitted his serene countenance, and the precious coffin revealed his golden arm.

When the mountain of Dharma collapsed, he swept away the arrows of Māra from the perilous screen; when the direct waters flowed crosswise, he moored the ferry of compassion on the other shore. Alas! How wondrous!
The treasury [of the Dharma] cannot remain perpetually concealed; the wheel of the precepts cannot ultimately be obstructed.

Although beneath the twin śāla trees, he manifested nirvāṇa, by the first millennium, his voice and teachings had spread abroad. Dragons held the palm leaves, frequently transmitting them through the city of Magadha;
elephants bore the lotus flowers, until they filled the realm of Zhendan (China). Thus, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment brought compassion to the burning house.
Twelve sutras draw metaphors from the sands of the world-systems.

As for the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, it was brought from Western India by Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan during the Later Han dynasty, as well as by the Dharma Master Xuanzang and Bodhiruci in the present day.
When the Tathāgata was formerly at Vulture Peak, establishing benefit and equality, his golden mouth poured forth [the teachings] like the ocean; one draws from this.

Yet it remains inexhaustible. The words of the Treasure (the Buddha) are like fine silk threads; when shaken, they reveal their continuity. These brilliant auspicious precepts have long been obscured at the Great Capital (Hongdu).

The valleys and ravines have repeatedly shifted, and the markets and courts have undergone many changes. Throughout successive dynasties, the rulers of Qi and the various states vied with one another to promote translations, yet the words of Bhadra’s prophecy were rarely brought to full completion.
Now that our Tang has possessed the empire, its merit spans the Iron Ring Mountains.

Transforming the Tuṣita Heaven and governing the thousandfold world-systems, they extend their dominion over ten thousand lands. Opening the gates of the four *saṃgrahavastus*, they widely receive all beings;

galloping upon the steeds of the six realms, they secretly deliver the multitudes of the deluded. His Majesty the Retired Emperor, whose benevolence is as deep as the ocean of wisdom, holds the radiant *dhyāna*-pearl in his hand.

His Majesty the Divine Emperor, whose merit reaches the Brahma-heaven, bears the *dharmamudrā* suspended upon his breast. He solemnly disseminates the profound edicts, illuminating and sprinkling grace.

Hongbo, having extensively selected from among the monastic community and clearly elucidated the various sections, conducted a thorough examination of similarities and differences, and thus initiated this compilation.
He courageously revitalized the sagging discipline and strictly upheld the severed bonds.

Therein were the śramaṇa of great virtue, Sijing, and the chief minister and Brahmin of East India, Īśvara, who translated the Sanskrit text; they sought the conditions for abiding in goodness and realized non-arising.
Ren (Ren-ru) possessed vast learning and a powerful memory; he translated it with meticulous precision.

Furthermore, there were the Indian śramaṇas Prajñākuṭa and Dharma, who verified the Sanskrit meanings, established the field of forbearance, shattered the hosts of afflictions, and harmonized with their divine companions as they clarified and distinguished the text.
Additionally, there were the śramaṇas of great virtue Lìfāng, Zōngyī, Pǔjìng, Huìjué, and others who served as scribes.
[He] caused [the disciples] to hear the teachings thoroughly and their deportment to be without error. Holding the celestial tablets in his hand, he received them and transcribed them.

Furthermore, there were śramaṇas of great virtue—Shenliang, Shengzhuang, Chenwai, Wuzhuo, Huidi, and others—who served as commentators on the meaning; they were the Great Masters of the land and the right arm of the Buddha.
They investigated the various definitive meanings and expounded and verified them. Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa of great virtue, Cheng... [text ends].

As for the sequence of the texts by Li Yunguan, Shen Jian, Dao Ben, and others: having sought refuge under the shade of many forests and rested my shoulders in fragrant caves, I have diligently applied myself with vigor to compile and arrange them.

Furthermore, there was an official who polished the text: Lu Can, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Yinqing Guanglu Dafu), Tutor to the Prince of Bin, Marquis of Gu'an County with the rank of Shangzhuguo.
Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Director of the Imperial Secretariat... [text continues].
Xu Jian, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Academician of the Chongwen Pavilion, concurrently Compiler of the National History, Marquis of Donghai Commandery with the rank of Shangzhuguo;
Su Jin, Grand Master for Court Deliberations, Acting Secretary of the Zhongshu Secretariat, Academician of the Chongwen Pavilion, Marquis of Shu Wang County with the rank of Shangzhuguo;
and Cui Qu, Grand Master for Court Deliberations, Palace Aide, and Attendant at Court, and others.
Their ranks were at the Phoenix Court, and their reputations spread throughout the Chicken Garden. They distinguished the Two Truths and enriched them with their refined colors.

Furthermore, there were Wei Zhigu, Grand Master of Imperial Secretariat (Jingguang Boluodafu), Acting Minister (Shizhong), concurrently Assistant to the Crown Prince (Taizi Zuoshuzi), concurrently Compiler of the National History (Xiuguo Shi), and Marquis of Julu County (Shangzhuguo);
and Guo Yuanzhen, Minister of War (Bingshu Shangshu) and Marquis of Shangzhuguo. Silver...
Zhang Yue, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Retained Rank of Director of the Secretariat, Merit of the Upper Pillar State, and Marquis of Fanyang County; Lu Xiangxian,
Grand Master of Splendid Green Happiness serving as Vice Director of the Secretariat, Concurrently of the Third Rank of the Palace Gate and Council of State,
Supervisor of the National History, and Merit of the Upper Pillar State, and Marquis of Xingping County, and others— having entered the inner gates of the court.

In the evening, he traveled through the realm of pearls. He upheld the four dharmas and reviewed them in their entirety. Thereupon, those who carry the mendicant’s staff and the eminent scholars of refined virtue were arrayed like hemp stalks at the fixed seats;
they gathered like forests in this land of bliss. Beneath auspicious clouds, he expounded and translated the scriptures until, in a flash, the seasons shifted from heat to cold.
Inhalating the nectar of the Dharma, he sought it with diligence. As the hours grew long, the chapters and verses of the Mahāyāna did not fail in their significance;
the subtle essence of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* rescued all without leaving anyone behind. His task was complete. What more could the Buddha have said?
The newly translated scriptures now comprise forty-nine assemblies and seventy-seven chapters, totaling twelve fascicles, arranged according to their categories and transcribed.
All having been completed, on the thirtieth day of the sixth month of the second year of the Xiāntiān era, [the scriptures] were presented to the Retired Emperor (Tàishànghuáng).

On the twenty-first day of the eighth month, they were presented to the Emperor. The inner palace gates opened at dawn, and the True Teaching was heard above. The celestial abodes were brought to joy, and the imperial heart was truly harmonious.

He stood solemnly upon the pivot of the state during the bright day, personally ascending the Altar of Spirits; he let fall clouds and rain from the crimson heavens, repeatedly bestowing extraordinary favors.

The Commandant, both the wise and the ignorant, bow their heads in reverence, regarding this as a favorable opportunity to behold the Benevolent King; both those in the ultimate and conventional realms turn their hearts toward him, regarding this as a secret ascent upon the path to enlightenment.

Following them are the lay Buddhist disciples, headed by Li Shiyuan, former Vice Director of the Office of the Imperial Household, who is the son of Li Huixiu—the late Imperial Court Grand Master of Golden Radiance and Minister of War, posthumously titled the Marquis of Longxi—and others. Furthermore...
There was a lay Buddhist disciple, Xu Yi (徐鐈), formerly a Right Reminder (You Shiyi) of the Court of Imperial Secretaries. His courtesy name was Gaoping Gong;
he held the rank of Silver Light Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments and was a Palace Attendant and Scholar of the Zhaowen Hall during the Imperial Dynasty.

As his private family had fallen into ruin due to a calamity sent down from the high heavens, he ascended the distant heights of the ancestral mounds with a broken heart and gazed toward the path of the unseen realm to offer merit. Thereupon, he opened [the treasury]...
Searching through chests and baskets, one finds the *Dānapāramitā*. Upon unfolding the broad layers of paper and scrolls, one first honors the act of transcription.

Before the fire of the *huái* tree has even changed its color, the volumes already fill the moss-covered covers. Thereafter, they are bound with carved rollers and fastened with jade labels; spread upon variegated mats, they unfurl like rainbows, and placed within pearl-encrusted cases, they are as richly adorned as brocade.
Only then can it be ensured that even if a fierce wind blows the mountains, the texts that open the path shall endure forever, and even if the kalpa-fire burns—
O Deva, do not destroy the Tārā scriptures.
